name: Avara Real Estate
description: A Sri Lankan property platform spanning rentals, property sales and short-term bookings with role-based users, geospatial search, availability, booking workflows, payments and property operations.
footer: The product combines discovery, transactions and operations: hosts, tenants, property calendars, bookings, media, local payments and administrative control.
users: Property seekers, tenants, hosts and administrators.
scope: Property discovery, transactions and host operations in Sri Lanka.
features: Rental, sale and short-stay listings with location and geospatial search.
Role-aware property administration and media uploads.
Availability calendars, booking workflows and local payment integration.
workflow: A visitor searches listings and opens a property.
An authenticated user submits a booking request; server-side rules evaluate availability.
Booking and payment state are stored in MongoDB; media is stored separately.
Hosts and administrators manage listings, calendars and transaction status.
boundary: This diagram summarizes the repository’s property, booking and payment boundaries. PayHere and S3 require deployment-specific configuration.
components: Customer, host and admin interfaces plus authenticated domain routes.
Users, properties, bookings and availability data.
Payment initiation and server-side notification handling.

name: Blu.lk
description: A Sri Lankan home-services platform connecting customers with skilled professionals across electrical, plumbing, cleaning, AC, carpentry and other services, with customer, provider and worker-facing workflows.
architecture: Customer + provider experiences → Laravel API → MySQL
footer: The product problem is trust plus operations: service discovery, scheduling, pricing, status, worker assignment and fulfillment all need to remain visible and manageable.
users: Customers, service providers, workers and operations teams.
scope: Home-service discovery, booking and fulfillment in Sri Lanka.
features: Service categories and customer booking journeys.
Provider and worker coordination around scheduled jobs.
Administrative management of services, users and operational status.
workflow: A customer discovers a service and supplies booking details.
The Laravel platform records the request and its status in MySQL.
Providers and workers coordinate assignment and fulfillment through their product experiences.
Operations teams manage service records and follow the booking lifecycle.
boundary: This diagram covers the core service platform. Payment-provider availability depends on integration configuration; no specific online payment launch is claimed here.
components: Booking, provider, worker and administrative workflows.

name: FreshPick / FreshOnTime
description: A premium food-commerce platform for Colombo bringing together fresh groceries, local products, prepared meals, recurring delivery and business ordering in one customer experience.
architecture: Next.js → Prisma / PostgreSQL → recurring delivery + media storage
footer: The direction goes beyond a grocery catalog: curation, repeat purchasing, convenience, recommendations and long-term customer relationships are part of the product system.
users: Grocery shoppers, local producers, business buyers and administrators.
scope: Food commerce, producer onboarding and scheduled recurring deliveries in Colombo.
features: Catalog browsing, product discovery and customer shopping.
Producer onboarding, admin operations and business enquiries.
Subscription baskets and recurring-order delivery scheduling.
Public read-only catalog tools through MCP.
workflow: A shopper chooses catalog items or a recurring basket.
Next.js validates the request and domain services persist orders through Prisma.
PostgreSQL holds catalog, order and delivery state; scheduling advances due deliveries.
Media and transactional messages use their configured storage and email integrations.
boundary: Customer checkout and subscription baskets currently use cash on delivery. Automatic recurring card charging is not implemented. Subscription baskets and recurring grocery orders are distinct workflows.
components: Storefront, producer and admin interfaces, API routes and public MCP catalog access.
Catalog, order, subscription and delivery records.

name: TimelyHelp.lk
description: A mental-healthcare platform for discovering licensed practitioners, booking secure consultations and managing digital care journeys. I worked on the product and frontend experience across practitioner discovery, account flows, checkout, dashboards and consultation surfaces.
architecture: Next.js 15 → NextAuth → practitioner APIs → Zoom Video SDK
footer: The frontend brings practitioner data, protected user flows, responsive product UI, monitoring and live consultation capabilities into one patient-facing experience.
users: People seeking mental-health consultations, practitioners and administrators.
scope: Product and frontend work for practitioner discovery and consultation journeys.
features: Practitioner discovery, accounts and protected dashboard flows.
Booking and checkout interfaces around consultation services.
Video-consultation surfaces, internationalization and frontend monitoring.
workflow: A visitor explores practitioner information.
NextAuth manages frontend authentication and protected account flows.
The frontend exchanges practitioner and consultation data with application APIs.
Video consultation uses Zoom Video SDK; Sentry supports frontend error visibility.
boundary: Savi’s portfolio contribution is product and frontend work. This page summarizes that frontend boundary and does not claim ownership of the full clinical backend.
components: Discovery, account, checkout, dashboard and consultation experiences.
Practitioner and consultation data supplied to the frontend.
Live video surfaces and error monitoring.

name: DevRelOS
description: An operating system for discovering developer signals, managing community and content workflows, connecting developer feedback to product work, and measuring outcomes from one operational surface.
architecture: Next.js → Go API → PostgreSQL → Workers → MCP
footer: Built around provider interfaces, evidence provenance, approval-gated side effects, observable automation and PostgreSQL as the system of record.
scope: A self-hosted beta for discovery, engagement and outcome measurement.
features: Signal Radar, pain-point intelligence and developer feedback.
Events, CFPs, reusable talks, contacts and relationships.
Content, campaigns, media workflows and approval-gated outreach.
Authenticated MCP tools and workspace-scoped access.
workflow: Connectors or an operator bring source-backed signals into a workspace.
The Go API validates membership and stores domain state in PostgreSQL.
Background workers run connector, media and approved outreach tasks.
The dashboard and MCP clients inspect work and track its outcomes through the domain API.
boundary: This project is a self-hosted beta. External providers require credentials and policy configuration; consequential outreach follows approval workflows.
components: Operator workspaces and same-origin API proxy.
Authenticated workflows, membership checks and business rules.
Workspace data, evidence, workflow state and audit history.
Connector ingestion, media rendering and approved delivery.
Authenticated domain tools; no parallel database access path.

name: Property Management OS
description: A rental operations platform covering properties, units, tenants, leases, rent, maintenance, documents, notifications and controlled agent-assisted operations.
architecture: Next.js → Go modular monolith → PostgreSQL → Outbox worker → MCP
footer: Domain rules live server-side: tenant isolation, RBAC, auditable rent ledgers, transactional notification delivery and authenticated agent tools.
users: Property managers, owners and authorized operational users.
scope: Multi-tenant rental operations and controlled agent-assisted work.
features: Properties, units, tenants, occupancies and leases.
Rent obligations, ledger views, maintenance and documents.
Organization membership, RBAC and audit-aware workflows.
Transactional notification outbox and authenticated MCP tools.
workflow: A manager or agent requests an operation through the authenticated API.
The Go modular monolith applies organization scope and domain rules.
PostgreSQL stores records and notification intents; documents use S3-compatible storage.
A Go worker consumes the outbox and delivers notifications through configured providers.
boundary: MCP calls the same authenticated HTTP API as other clients and has no direct database connection. Advanced financial writes and other domains remain subject to the project’s implemented tool scope.
components: Organization-scoped domain logic, OIDC identity and RBAC.
Portfolio, tenancy, rent, maintenance and outbox state.
Durable notification processing through a delivery provider.
Agent access through authenticated domain APIs.

name: RapidReach
description: A developer publication and tool-discovery product with editorial workflows, comments, likes, search, tool profiles, media uploads and a deliberately small CMS.
footer: The product keeps deployment simple while still exposing structured data, feeds, APIs, sitemap, robots and llms.txt for search engines, answer engines and agents.
users: Readers, developers exploring tools and editorial administrators.
scope: Developer publishing and tool discovery with a small CMS.
features: Articles, categories, search, comments, likes and sharing.
Tool profiles, category browsing and tool upvotes.
Editorial draft/publish workflows and media uploads.
Structured metadata, feeds and machine-readable discovery surfaces.
workflow: An editor creates a draft and attaches uploaded media.
The CMS stores editorial and tool records in MongoDB.
Published pages and tool profiles render from the same Next.js application.
Readers discover content through the site, search and published feeds.
boundary: RapidReach uses one Next.js application with MongoDB and Blob storage; there is no separate backend service. Publishing and media require a configured deployment.
components: Public pages, tool directory, CMS and API routes in one application.
Editorial records, tool records, comments and categories.
Public media objects referenced by content records.

name: Advance HRIS
description: A hybrid HR information system with an employee web portal, a native HR/admin desktop console, tenant-scoped access, policy-backed leave, schedule-aware attendance, audit history and durable offline synchronization.
architecture: Next.js Web + Wails / React Desktop → Go API → PostgreSQL
footer: The system combines cloud-authoritative HR data with a local-first desktop workflow, encrypted local payloads, conflict-aware sync and payroll-ready attendance boundaries.
users: Employees, managers, HR teams and administrators.
scope: Hybrid web and local-first desktop HR operations.
features: Employee records, tenant scope and role-aware self-service.
Policy-backed leave and schedule-aware attendance.
Audit history and durable offline desktop synchronization.
workflow: Employees and managers use the Next.js portal for self-service.
HR/admin users can work through the Wails desktop console and local SQLite storage.
The durable sync queue sends authorized operations to the Go API.
PostgreSQL remains the authoritative system of record; synchronization handles conflicts explicitly.
boundary: Local-first refers to the desktop console. The cloud database remains authoritative. Payroll-ready attendance boundaries do not mean a complete payroll-processing product is included.
components: Employee and manager self-service through a web session/BFF boundary.
Native HR/admin console with encrypted local payloads.
Local state and durable synchronization operations.
Tenant-scoped business rules and authoritative HR records.

name: NexusPOS
description: A retail POS and store-operations system covering touch checkout, barcode workflows, inventory, staff roles, cash shifts, refunds, reconciliation, audit history and native receipt printing.
footer: Built as more than a checkout screen: the system handles stock-safe transactions, cash-drawer operations, refunds, reporting and multi-platform desktop packaging.
users: Cashiers, store managers and retail administrators.
scope: Checkout and store operations with an optional Electron desktop shell.
features: Touch checkout, barcode/SKU input, held orders and receipts.
Inventory, authenticated staff roles and store settings.
Cash shifts, refunds, reconciliation and audit history.
workflow: A cashier builds a basket and applies eligible discounts or loyalty.
Authenticated server routes calculate checkout totals and validate stock.
Prisma persists retail records to MongoDB.
The optional Electron shell provides native receipt printing while the browser supports print fallback.
boundary: Electron is an optional desktop shell. The portfolio does not claim a complete offline checkout engine or a tenant-isolated hosted retail service.
components: Authenticated staff actions and server-authoritative checkout.
Products, orders and retail operational records.
Optional native desktop packaging and receipt printing.

name: Academix
description: A SaaS workspace for tuition centres and private institutes combining student CRM, classes, attendance, assessments, fee collection, communications, reporting and multi-site institute operations.
footer: The product consolidates academic and operational workflows into a role-aware workspace with SaaS plan surfaces, reporting and extensible notification integrations.
users: Tuition centres, academies and private-institute staff.
scope: Student, academic and fee operations in a role-aware workspace.
features: Student CRM, enrollments, teacher and class records.
Manual, bulk and barcode attendance plus assessments.
Fees, LKR receipts, reporting and institute records.
Communication workflows with email/SMS integration points.
workflow: Staff register students and enroll them into classes.
Authenticated application routes record attendance, grades and fee activity.
Mongoose models store operational records in MongoDB.
Dashboards and reports summarize the workspace; communication providers are configured separately.
boundary: The account and plan surfaces support a SaaS direction. Automated billing and broader tenant-isolation work should be checked against the current project roadmap rather than assumed complete.
components: Student, academic, fee, communication and reporting workspaces.
Cookie-based JWT sessions and role-aware domain requests.
Student, class, attendance, assessment and fee records.
Configured email/SMS providers; integration availability varies by deployment.

name: Acme Accounting
description: A single-company accounting application with a double-entry general ledger, invoicing, A/R and A/P aging, vendor bills, credit notes, refunds, period locks, bank reconciliation, budgeting and financial reporting.
footer: Accounting integrity is enforced at the posting layer with balanced journals, reversible history, period controls and ledger-backed financial statements instead of dashboard-only bookkeeping.
users: A company’s accounting administrator and finance operator.
scope: Single-company financial operations backed by a double-entry ledger.
features: Chart of accounts, journals, invoicing and receivables.
Vendor bills, payables, expenses, credit notes and refunds.
Bank reconciliation, period locks, recurring transactions and budgets.
Ledger-backed statements and accounting integrity diagnostics.
workflow: An operator creates a source document such as an invoice or vendor bill.
Authenticated domain services validate the accounting transition.
The posting layer records balanced journals in the general ledger.
Reports read the ledger while period controls and audit history preserve traceability.
boundary: The current application is designed for one company and one administrator identity per database. It is not a tenant-isolated accounting SaaS backend.
components: Finance interfaces and authenticated route handlers.
Source-document workflows, validation and period controls.
Balanced journal posting, reversal and source-level idempotency.
Financial records, journal history and reporting source data.

name: EventOS
description: An event-services marketplace and operations platform for finding suppliers, comparing quotes, managing bookings and contracts, tracking payments and coordinating event delivery.
architecture: Next.js → PostgreSQL → transactional workflows + file storage
footer: Two connected journeys: quick service matching and full event procurement with buyer, supplier and admin workflows.
users: Guests, event buyers, suppliers and administrators.
scope: Quick provider matching and full event procurement.
features: Service requests, supplier profiles and quote comparison.
Bookings, contracts and event execution workflows.
Manual payment submission and administrative reconciliation.
PostgreSQL sessions, row-level authorization and persistent uploads.
workflow: A guest requests a provider or a buyer defines an event and service requirements.
Suppliers submit quotes; the buyer compares and accepts an offer.
Database transactions coordinate booking, contract and commercial state.
Authorized users share files and track execution; administrators reconcile submitted payment records.
boundary: Payments are submitted and reconciled manually in the current MVP. This is a Next.js and PostgreSQL application; a Supabase service is not required for the documented runtime.
components: Public marketplace and buyer, supplier and admin workflows.
Sessions, row-level authorization, functions and lifecycle state.
Public supplier assets and access-controlled event documents.

name: Plate Restaurant OS
description: A restaurant-management product bringing point of sale, table service, direct online ordering, kitchen workflows, menus and inventory into one operational workspace.
footer: The product coordinates orders between customer-facing ordering, restaurant staff and kitchen operations.
users: Restaurant staff, kitchen teams, managers and direct-order customers.
scope: Restaurant point of sale and coordinated order operations.
features: POS, table management and menu administration.
Direct online ordering and kitchen display workflows.
Inventory and operational analytics.
workflow: A customer or staff member creates an order.
Authenticated Next.js routes validate the request and persist the order.
Kitchen and staff interfaces coordinate preparation and service.
Managers maintain menus and inventory and inspect order reports.
boundary: The product is under development. POS, kitchen and online ordering share a Next.js application and MongoDB data layer; external integrations require deployment-specific configuration.
components: Ordering, POS, kitchen, menu and manager surfaces.
Restaurant, menu, order and inventory records.

name: Pain Intelligence Lab
description: A cross-source research platform for discovering repeated customer pain, costly workarounds and product opportunities using saved evidence, quality checks and an MCP-connected research host.
architecture: React / Vite + MCP host → Express API → MongoDB
footer: Research conclusions remain connected to sources, independent stories, competing explanations and validation work.
users: Builders, product teams and market researchers.
scope: Cross-source pain research and evidence-backed opportunity validation.
features: Manual evidence ingestion and native Reddit deep research.
Autonomous research jobs executed by a connected MCP host.
Semantic clustering, jobs-to-be-done and opportunity synthesis.
Source diversity, duplicate checks and competitor/pricing validation.
workflow: A researcher creates a market question and research job.
The MCP host gathers evidence and sends it through the platform’s tool boundary.
Express stores evidence and workflow state in MongoDB and applies quality/scoring checks.
Host reasoning annotates and clusters evidence before opportunities are validated or rejected.
boundary: The application does not call model-provider APIs directly; semantic reasoning runs in the connected MCP host. A research job may correctly produce no validated opportunity.
components: Research questions, saved evidence and project inspection.
Storage, evidence-quality scoring and workflow state.
Browsing, annotation, semantic reasoning and synthesis.
Evidence, research projects, snapshots and job state.

name: Ad Performance Analysis Agent
description: A campaign-performance analysis prototype that parses ad-data CSVs, compares weekly metrics, highlights risks and wins, and uses Gemini to help produce actionable summaries.
architecture: React / Vite → Express → CSV analysis + Gemini → email
footer: CSV analysis is implemented. Google Ads and Supermetrics connections are mocked; the scheduled demo uses sample data.
users: Marketing operators and teams reviewing campaign performance.
scope: An advertising analytics and reporting prototype.
features: CSV parsing of campaign dates, spend, clicks, impressions and conversions.
Week-over-week metrics and threshold-based risk/win flags.
Gemini-assisted summaries and email reporting paths.
workflow: An operator supplies campaign data as CSV.
The analysis module normalizes rows and compares current and previous periods.
Threshold logic identifies risks and wins; Gemini helps summarize next steps.
The reporting interface displays results and the email path can send a summary when configured.
boundary: Google Ads and Supermetrics connection endpoints are currently mocks. Scheduled demonstration runs use generated sample CSVs and in-memory configuration, rather than a durable live account-ingestion pipeline.
components: Prototype configuration, scheduling and reporting endpoints.
CSV normalization, weekly comparison and threshold flags.
Configured AI summarization and email-report delivery.

name: MediCare
description: A patient and clinic-management system covering patient administration, appointments, clinical records, billing, staff permissions and an embeddable scheduling service.
architecture: Next.js → Go API + scheduling service → PostgreSQL
footer: Patient, clinical, billing and administrative workflows use separate server-enforced permissions.
users: Clinic staff, doctors, billing operators, administrators and patients.
scope: Patient administration, appointments, clinical records and billing.
features: Patient profiles and conflict-aware appointment scheduling.
Clinical records with SOAP notes, vitals and prescriptions.
Billing records, payment tracking and operational dashboards.
Staff management and a separate embeddable scheduling API.
workflow: Clinic staff register a patient or arrange an appointment.
The Go API validates identity, role permissions and domain requests.
PostgreSQL stores patient, appointment, clinical and billing state.
A separate scheduling service supports website embeds within its intended scheduling boundary.
boundary: The main clinic API and embeddable scheduling API use separate service boundaries. Server-enforced roles separate clinical, billing and administrative access.
components: Patient, appointment, clinical, billing and admin interfaces.
JWT sessions, role checks and clinic workflows.
Separate service boundary for embeddable appointments.
Patient and operational records persisted by the backend.
